stories.title: Fires in Indonesia Could Send Haze to Singapore
stories.headline_kid: Huge wildfires are burning across Indonesia, and the smoke could soon drift over to Singapore.
summary: Indonesia is battling massive forest and land fires that have already burned about 107,000 hectares. That is bigger than the whole of Singapore, which is only about 73,000 hectares! Dry weather caused by a weather pattern called El Nino has made it much easier for these fires to start and spread.

President Prabowo Subianto has ordered many government agencies to work together to put out the fires. This is important not just for Indonesia, but for neighbouring countries too, because smoke from these fires can travel across borders and turn into hazy, smoky skies.
Singapore has faced this problem before. When haze levels rise, the air quality gets worse, and people — especially children and the elderly — may need to stay indoors or wear masks outdoors.
Right now, Indonesia is trying hard to stop the fires before they get worse. Singapore's National Environment Agency will keep a close watch on air quality in case the haze reaches us.

lenses.me: If haze levels rise, you might need to stay indoors during recess or wear a mask when outside.
lenses.family: Your family may need to check the PSI (air quality) readings and keep windows closed on hazy days.
lenses.friends: Outdoor sports, CCA training or school events could be cancelled or moved indoors if haze gets bad.
lenses.nation: Singapore works closely with Indonesia and other neighbours to tackle haze, since smoke doesn't respect borders.
lenses.world: This shows how one country's fires can affect the health and daily life of people in other countries far away.

stories.title: Get Ready for a Super Hot, Dry Spell in Singapore
stories.headline_kid: Scientists warn that an extremely strong El Nino could bring scorching heat and little rain to Singapore and the region.
summary: El Nino is a weather pattern where the Pacific Ocean becomes warmer than usual. Think of it like a switch that turns off rain clouds over Southeast Asia and turns up the heat instead. This year's El Nino is expected to be unusually strong — some experts even call it a 'super' El Nino.

Experts say this could cause drought, very hot days, and problems for farmers growing crops across Southeast Asia from 2026 into 2027. If crops fail, food prices could go up, which affects families everywhere, including in Singapore.

Governments across the region are already preparing plans to deal with the heat and dryness, but experts warn there are still many weak spots. Singapore may need to look out for water usage, heat safety at schools, and higher electricity bills from more air-conditioning use.
For now, the best thing families can do is stay informed, drink more water, and be extra careful during outdoor activities when the weather turns very hot.

lenses.me: You might feel much hotter during outdoor PE lessons or CCA training, so remember to drink more water and wear a hat.
lenses.family: Your family's water and electricity bills might go up because of more air-conditioner use during hot spells.
lenses.friends: Schools may adjust outdoor activity timings to avoid the hottest parts of the day.
lenses.nation: Singapore may need to activate heat and water-saving plans, and rely more on NEWater and desalinated water.
lenses.world: Extreme heat and drought can hurt farming across Southeast Asia, which could raise food prices for everyone.

stories.title: Bali Cracks Down on Influencers Making Money While on Holiday
stories.headline_kid: Bali is checking more strictly on foreign influencers who earn money from videos while on a tourist visa.
summary: Many foreign travellers visit Bali on tourist visas just for holidays. But some of them also film content, get paid by brands, or earn money from social media — even though their visa does not allow them to work or run a business there.
Indonesian authorities in Bali are now tightening their checks on this. People who break the rules could be fined or even sent home early.
This has led to calls for clearer visa rules, so that content creators know exactly what they can and cannot do while visiting.

Many Singaporeans love visiting Bali for holidays, and some even film travel vlogs there. This news is a good reminder that every country has its own rules, and it's important to follow them wherever you travel.

lenses.me: If you ever make videos on holiday, this reminds you that different countries have different rules about what tourists can do.
lenses.family: Families planning a Bali holiday might want to check the latest travel rules before flying off.
lenses.friends: Friends who enjoy watching travel vlogs from Bali might notice creators being more careful about what they post.
lenses.nation: It's a good reminder for Singaporean travellers to respect the laws of the countries they visit.
lenses.world: It shows how the rise of influencers and social media is pushing many countries to update old visa rules.

stories.title: Pilot's Drug Test Raises Big Questions About Flight Safety
stories.headline_kid: A pilot whose plane suddenly dropped in the sky has tested positive for a banned drug, raising serious safety concerns.
summary: Last week, an Air India flight travelling from Phuket to Delhi suddenly lost about 300 feet of height in the sky — roughly the height of a 30-storey building. This sudden drop hurt 13 passengers and 4 crew members onboard.

Investigators have now confirmed that the flight's captain tested positive for marijuana, a drug that can affect a person's focus and reaction time. Pilots are strictly not allowed to fly under the influence of such substances, because even a small mistake at high altitude can be dangerous.
Aircraft maker Airbus has now joined the investigation to find out exactly what caused the plane to drop so suddenly, and whether the pilot's condition played a part.

This story is a strong reminder of why airlines have such strict safety and health checks for pilots. Singapore's aviation authorities also enforce tough rules to keep flights through Changi Airport safe for everyone.

lenses.me: It's a reminder that flying is generally very safe because pilots go through many strict checks before every flight.
lenses.family: Your family can feel reassured knowing that airlines have rules to catch unsafe pilots before they fly.
lenses.friends: This might spark a chat with friends about what should happen to pilots who break important safety rules.
lenses.nation: Singapore's aviation authority (CAAS) also enforces strict drug and health checks for pilots flying in and out of Changi.
lenses.world: This incident is pushing airlines worldwide to review how carefully they check pilots' health before flights.

stories.title: Digger Engines Power the World's Fastest Hydrogen Car
stories.headline_kid: A car built using engines from diggers just set a world speed record — and it runs on clean hydrogen fuel, not petrol!
summary: Former fighter pilot Andy Green has set a new world land speed record for a hydrogen-powered vehicle. He drove the JCB Hydromax car across the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, USA, reaching incredibly high speeds using two engines that were originally designed for digger machines used in construction!
Hydrogen is special because when it powers an engine, it mostly produces water vapour instead of the smoky pollution that petrol engines create. That makes it a much cleaner way to power vehicles.
This record shows that even everyday machines, like the engines inside diggers, can be turned into something record-breaking with clever engineering and a bit of imagination.

Singapore is also exploring hydrogen as a clean fuel for future buses, trucks, and even ships, as part of our push to reduce pollution. This world record is a fun reminder of how far clean technology can go.

lenses.friends: This could spark fun conversations with friends about what clean, futuristic vehicles might look like.
lenses.nation: Singapore is studying hydrogen fuel for public buses and ships, so this record hints at what's possible for us too.
lenses.world: Breakthroughs like this help push hydrogen technology forward, which could reduce pollution from vehicles everywhere.
